:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
On a particular day, the rate $E$ at which tourists enter a small country can be modeled as $E(t) = 50\cdot 3^{0.2t}$ tourists per hour, where $t$ is the time, in hours, after midnight. The rate at which tourists leave the country can be modeled as $L(t)=100\cdot 2^{0.2t}$ tourists per hour, where $t$ is also the time in hours after midnight.

What is the rate of change in the number of tourists in the country at $10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of the number of tourists in the country at time $t$ is equal to the entry rate minus the exit rate at time $t,$ that is, 

$$
E(t)-L(t).
$$

Since $10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}$ is ten hours after midnight, we have $t=10.$ Substituting $t=10,$ the rate of change in the number of tourists in the country at $10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}E(10)-L(10) & =50\cdot {3}^{0.2(10)}-100\cdot {2}^{0.2(10)} \\  & =450-400 \\  & =50.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change in the number of tourists in the country at $10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}$ is $50$ tourists per hour.

The rate at which water is leaking from the pool can be modeled as $L(t) = \frac{1}{4}t^{2}$ liters per minute, where $t$ is also the time, in minutes, since the pool began to be filled.

After taking a pill containing $300$ milligrams of a particular drug, the quantity of the drug in a patient's body decreases at a rate of $c(t)=300\cdot {2}^{-0.7t}$ milligrams per hour, where $t$ is the time, in hours, since the patient consumed the pill. What will be the rate of decrease after $5$ hours? Round your answer to the nearest integer.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Since we want to determine the rate of decrease in the quantity of the drug in the patient's body after $5$ hours, we have $t=5.$

Thus, the rate of decrease in the quantity of the drug after $5$ hours will be

$$
\begin{aligned}c(5) & =300\cdot {2}^{-0.7(5)} \\  & =300\cdot {2}^{-3.5} \\  & \approx 27.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of decrease will be $27$ milligrams per hour.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
What was the exact rate of change of the stock's value at week $9?$

{{field-1}}$\,$ thousand dollars per week.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The function ${h}^{'}(x)$ models the rate of change of the value of the stock, applicable in the domain of $h(x).$

Thus, the rate of change of the value of the stock at $x=9$ weeks is

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{'}(9) & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 3} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change in the stock price was $\frac{1}{9}$ thousand dollars per week.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: The birth rate of a krill population is modeled by $B(t)=5\cdot {2}^{0.7t}$ thousands of tons per year, where $t$ is the time, in years, since $1998.$ What was the birth rate, in thousands of tons per year, for the krill in $2008?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The function $B(t)$ models the birth rate for the krill, in thousands of tons, $t$ years since $1998.$ Since we want the birth rate in $2008$, then $t=10$ years.

Thus, the birth rate for the krill in $2008$ was

$$
\begin{aligned}B(10) & =5\cdot {2}^{0.7(10)} \\  & =5\cdot {2}^{7} \\  & =640.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the birth rate for the krill in $2008$ was $640$ thousand tons per year.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: The decay rate $M$ of muons in a beam traveling at high speed can be modeled by the function $M(t)=2\cdot {e}^{-2t},$ where $t$ is the time, in microseconds, since observations started. What will be the decay rate of the muons after $0.5$ microseconds? Round your answer to three decimal places.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The function $M(t)$ models the decay rate for the particles $t$ microseconds since observations started.

Thus, the decay rate of the muons after $0.5$ microseconds is

$$
\begin{aligned}M(0.5) & =2\cdot {e}^{-2(0.5)} \\  & =2\cdot {e}^{-1} \\  & ≈0.736.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the decay rate of the particles is $0.736$ muons per microsecond.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: After charging the battery of a PC, the percentage of charge decreases at a rate of $c(t)=100\cdot {5}^{-0.2t}$ percent per hour, where $t$ is the time, in hours, since the battery had completed its charge. What will be the rate of decrease after $5$ hours?
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Since we want to determine the rate of decrease in the amount of charge after $5$ hours, we have $t=5.$

Thus, the rate of decrease of the amount of charge after $5$ hours will be

$$
\begin{aligned}c(5) & =100\cdot {5}^{-0.2(5)} \\  & =100\cdot {5}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{100}{5} \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of decrease will be $20$ percent per hour.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
The rate $O$ of the orders a car factory receives can be modeled as $O(t)=100t{e}^{-0.1t}$ cars per day. The rate at which cars are completed can be modeled as $C(t)=50+10sin⁡(\frac{2\pi }{7}t)$ cars per day. In both cases, $t$ is the time, in days, since the launch of the new model. 

What is the rate of change in the number of cars under construction $28$ days after the model's launch? Assume that an ordered car goes into construction as soon as the factory receives its order. Round your answer to the nearest integer.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of the number of cars under construction at time $t$ is equal to the order rate minus the completion rate, that is,

$$
O(t)-C(t).
$$

Substituting $t=28,$ the rate of change in the number of cars under construction after $28$ days is

$$
\begin{aligned}O(t)-C(t) & =100(28){e}^{-0.1(28)}-(50+10sin⁡(\frac{2\pi }{7}(28))) \\  & =100(28){e}^{-2.8}-50-10sin⁡(8\pi ) \\  & =100(28){e}^{-2.8}-50 \\  & ≈120.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change in the number of cars in construction after $28$ days is $120$ cars per day.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: The growth rate, $G(t)$, of the number of bacteria in a culture can be modeled by the function $G(t)=100\cdot {2}^{0.5t}$, where $t$ is the time, in hours, since a sample of bacteria was placed in a Petri dish.  What will be the growth rate of the bacteria after $6$ hours?
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The function $G(t)$ models the growth rate for the bacteria $t$ hours since the sample was put in the Petri dish.

Thus, the growth rate of the bacteria culture after $6$ hours is

$$
\begin{aligned}G(6) & =100\cdot {2}^{0.5(6)} \\  & =100\cdot {2}^{3} \\  & =100\cdot 8 \\  & =800.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the growth rate of the bacteria is $800$ bacteria per hour.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
The birth rate of a herd of elephants in a region in Africa is modeled by the function  $B(t)=500\cdot {2}^{0.125t}$ while the rate of death is modeled by $D(t)=400\cdot {3}^{0.125t}.$ In both cases, $t$ represents the number of years since $1990.$  

What was the rate of change of the elephant population in that region in $1998?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The  rate of change in the number of elephants  $t$ years since $1990$ is equal to the difference between the two given rates, that is

$$
B(t)-D(t).
$$

As $1998$ is $8$ years after $1990$, we have $t=8.$  Hence, the  rate of change in the elephant population in that region in $1998$ was 

$$
\begin{aligned}B(8)-D(8) & =500\cdot {2}^{0.125(8)}-400\cdot {3}^{0.125(8)} \\  & =500\cdot 2-400\cdot 3 \\  & =-200.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change in the elephant population was $-200$ elephants per year.
